sources.title: DrivenData - GEMS Prize Challenge: Problem description
used_for: the official definition of the distance-weighted Tversky index
alpha = 0.2, beta = 0.8, triangular kernel with R = 300 m (3 px at 100 m)
the submission format (single band, float32, values between 0 and 1, same CRS/resolution/bounds as the training data, null/nan outside the bounds)
the statement that the scored truth is expert-labelled faults NOT in the public USGS/INGENIOUS database
the list of provided features, including the top-of-crustal magnetic source depth estimate

verbatim.kernel: k(d) = (1 - d/R)_+ = max(1 - d/R, 0). where the range R is 300 meters (i.e., 3 pixels at 100m resolution).
verbatim.metrics: For this competition, we set alpha = 0.2 and beta = 0.8, which reduces the penalty for false positive predictions and increases the penalty for false negative predictions.
verbatim.format: Your submission contains a single layer with datatype of 32-bit float (float32) with values between 0 and 1 indicating the confidence or probability of fault presence, with higher values indicating higher probability.
verbatim.truth: the sponsors have compiled a set of newly identified faults in the GeoDAWN region that are not included in the existing USGS fault database. These new faults have been manually labeled by fault experts and comprise the test dataset for the competition.
verbatim.promised_band: Magnetics including reduced-to-pole magnetic anomaly, total magnetic intensity, the vertical and horizontal slope of total magnetic intensity, and the top-of-crustal magnetic source depth estimate

sources.discrepancy_found: The delivered 19-band raster does not contain the promised top-of-crustal magnetic source depth estimate. See docs/findings.html, irregularity I-4.

sources.title: Faulds, J.E., Hinz, N.H., Coolbaugh, M.F., et al. (2012) - Assessment of Favorable Structural Settings of Geothermal Systems in the Great Basin, Western USA. New Zealand Geothermal Workshop 2012 Proceedings.
sources.publisher: DOE Geothermal Data Repository (GDR) / University of Nevada
used_for: the structural-settings frequency distribution used to justify prioritising step-overs, terminations and intersections
sources.verbatim: Of the 250+ geothermal fields catalogued, step-overs or relay ramps in normal fault zones serve as the most favorable setting, hosting ~32% of the systems. ... Other common settings include a) intersections between normal faults and strike-slip or oblique-slip faults (22%) ... and b) normal fault terminations or tip-lines (22%) ... Other settings include accommodation zones (i.e., belts of intermeshing, oppositely dipping normal faults; 8%), major normal faults (6%), displacement transfer zones (5%), and pull-aparts in strike-slip faults (4%).
sources.scope_limit: These percentages describe where GEOTHERMAL SYSTEMS are located. The competition labels are expert-mapped FAULTS missing from the public catalogue. The two populations are not the same; this source motivates the structural hypotheses but does not establish them for the competition label set.

sources.title: Giddens, E. and Faulds, J.E. (2025) - Step-over characteristics in the Great Basin region. Proceedings, 50th Workshop on Geothermal Reservoir Engineering, Stanford University.
used_for: the quantitative relay-ramp width used to set the gap window in hypothesis H1
the strike preference used to justify a north to north-northeast oriented detector
verbatim: The most common structural setting for known geothermal systems in the Great Basin region is the step-over or relay ramp, which accounts for ~47% of all producing systems in Nevada and ~39% of all known Nevada geothermal systems
Over 73% of right-stepping step-overs reside on fault strands that strike north to north-northeast.
Approximately 17% of all the step-overs in the Great Basin region are associated with known geothermal systems.
These step-overs have an average relay ramp width of 2.1 km ... The average relay ramp width is 2.5 km ... average relay ramp width of 2.8 km

sources.verbatim: Structural controls of 426 geothermal systems in the Great Basin region ... were analyzed ... Of the systems analyzed, we were able to determine the structural settings of more than 240 sites.

sources.title: Faulds, J.E. and Hinz, N.H. (2015) - Favorable tectonic and structural settings of geothermal systems in the Great Basin region, western USA: Proxies for discovering blind geothermal systems. Proceedings World Geothermal Congress, Melbourne.
used_for: the 426-system / ~250 categorised figures and the ~32% step-over share quoted on the OSTI record
sources.verbatim: We recently completed a comprehensive inventory of the structural settings of known geothermal systems (426 total, >=37C) in the extensional to transtensional terrane of the Great Basin region in the western USA. ... Of the nearly 250 categorized geothermal fields, we found that step-overs or relay ramps in normal fault zones are the most favorable setting, hosting ~32% of the systems.

sources.title: Faulds, J.E. et al. (2014) - Favorable structural settings of active geothermal systems in the Great Basin region, western USA. GSA Annual Meeting, Vancouver, abstract.
used_for: the contrast between fault interaction zones and mid-segment displacement maxima
sources.verbatim: Of ~250 categorized fields, step-overs or relay ramps in normal fault zones are the most favorable setting, hosting ~32% of the systems. ... b) fault intersections (22%) ... and c) accommodation zones (9%) ... The primary segments of major faults only host ~1% of the geothermal fields.

The files themselves could NOT be downloaded from this sandbox: every non-GitHub host (sciencebase.gov, earthexplorer.usgs.gov, prd-tnm.s3.amazonaws.com, gdr.openei.org, pubs.usgs.gov) fails to complete a TLS handshake here. Availability is therefore confirmed from the catalogue record, not by download. See limitations.

sources.title: DrivenData community forum thread 11516 - Scoring clarification: are known USGS/INGENIOUS faults masked when scoring, and are they in the final round label set?
used_for: the masking behaviour implemented in src/gems/holdout.py mask_mode='pixel_exact'
sources.provenance_note: The URL is recorded as the citation for pixel-exact masking in the sibling repository's own measurement ledger (5GEMSDOE data/evidence/leaderboard_anchor/leaderboard_anchor.json, key 'sources.known_faults_masked_from_scoring'), which was read directly in this session. The thread text itself was not retrieved here, so the masking rule is treated as an externally supplied premise, not as something verified by this repository.

unverified_claims_deliberately_not_asser: The user-supplied sentence that roughly a third of Great Basin geothermal systems sit at fault step-overs and 'another fifth each at terminations and intersections' is consistent with the Faulds sources above (~32% / ~22% / ~22%) and is therefore recorded as sourced, but the framing that this frequency transfers to the competition's missing-fault label population is NOT established by any source read here.

No source read in this session states what the DrivenData validator's exact range check is. The '[0, 1]' requirement quoted on the submission form and the problem description is used as the specification; the failure that produced the operator's error message was not reproduced from any published artifact (see docs/findings.html, irregularity I-6).
The public/private chunking of the competition region is not published anywhere read here.
